title: D-State (Uninterruptible Sleep) Process Detection
exclusions: Detects a Linux process identity sampled with a leading `D` state in three consecutive selected `ps` snapshots. It does not prove that the task remained continuously blocked between polls, determine whether storage, a network filesystem, a device driver, memory reclaim, or another kernel wait is responsible, measure service impact, inspect tasks that start and finish between polls, or independently resolve container PID namespaces. The supplied `ps.sh` fields do not provide a reliable process-start identity, and the primary SPL has no exception lookup or compliance claim.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_process_d_state_persistence_15m` saved-search definition, schedule and alert history, returned host/PID/command/user and three-bucket measurements, the three underlying `sourcetype=ps` snapshots, and the associated incident record. These artifacts show that indexed samples met the configured persistence rule; they do not prove continuous uninterruptible sleep, complete collection, root cause, or remediation.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index with the `Splunk_TA_nix` search-time knowledge, index three complete aligned `sourcetype=ps` table snapshots for `host=dstate-positive` in three adjacent closed five-minute buckets. In every snapshot include `PID=4242`, `COMMAND=io-worker`, `USER=svc_test`, and a `STAT` value beginning with `D` (`D`, `D<`, and `Ds` are valid examples), plus at least one healthy process row. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds. Expect exactly one row for PID 4242 with `observed_buckets=3`, `dstate_buckets=3`, and `sample_span_minutes=10`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Index three equivalent snapshots for `host=dstate-negative`, but set PID 5252 to `STAT=D`, `STAT=S`, and `STAT=D` in chronological order. Expect zero final rows; immediately before the final `where`, confirm `observed_buckets=3` and `dstate_buckets=2`. Also test a different D-state PID in each bucket and a healthy `S` process whose command contains the letter D; neither case may alert.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=ps` multi-line process-table snapshots produced by the `ps.sh` scripted event input supplied with the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). The search selects the latest raw snapshot in each closed five-minute bucket before `multikv` expands its rows. Required current Linux columns are `PID`, `STAT`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`; documented legacy `S` is accepted in place of `STAT`. `_time` and `host` are Splunk metadata. The index and five-minute interval are deployment choices.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), installed on Linux collection forwarders and on the Splunk tiers that require its parsing and search-time knowledge.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=ps host=* earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval snapshot_time=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| eventstats max(snapshot_time) as selected_snapshot_time by _time host
| where snapshot_time=selected_snapshot_time
| multikv
| eval process_id=trim(tostring(coalesce(PID,pid,process_id))), process_state=upper(trim(tostring(coalesce(STAT,S,stat)))), process_name=trim(coalesce(COMMAND,command,process_name,"(command unavailable)")), process_user=trim(coalesce(USER,user,process_user,"(user unavailable)"))
| where match(process_id,"^[0-9]+$") AND match(process_state,"^[A-Z]")
| stats latest(process_state) as process_state latest(process_user) as process_user by _time host process_id process_name
| eval is_d_state=if(match(process_state,"^D"),1,0)
| stats count as observed_buckets sum(is_d_state) as dstate_buckets values(process_state) as observed_states earliest(_time) as first_bucket latest(_time) as last_bucket latest(process_user) as process_user by host process_id process_name
| eval required_buckets=3, required_dstate_buckets=3, required_sample_span_seconds=600, sample_span_seconds=last_bucket-first_bucket, sample_span_minutes=round(sample_span_seconds/60,1)
| where observed_buckets=required_buckets AND dstate_buckets=required_dstate_buckets AND sample_span_seconds=required_sample_span_seconds
| convert ctime(first_bucket) ctime(last_bucket)
| table first_bucket last_bucket host process_id process_name process_user observed_states observed_buckets dstate_buckets sample_span_minutes required_buckets required_dstate_buckets
| sort 0 host process_id
description: Reports a Linux process only when the same host, numeric PID, and command is present with a leading `D` process state in the latest complete sample from each of three consecutive closed five-minute buckets. It parses the add-on's multi-line table and treats the result as repeated observations, not proof that the task was continuously blocked between polls.
value: Repeatedly observing one task in uninterruptible sleep can expose a serious kernel-side wait before blocked work exhausts worker pools, stalls dependent requests, or makes a host difficult to drain or stop. Process-level persistence removes fleeting one-snapshot waits and rotating unrelated tasks from the alert, shortening storage, filesystem, device, and kernel triage by preserving the task identity operators need.
implementation: Enable the add-on's supplied `ps.sh` scripted event input on Linux forwarders, route complete process-table events to the deliberately selected `os` index, and collect every five minutes. Verify that `multikv` yields numeric `PID`, current `STAT` or legacy `S`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`. Schedule the saved search every five minutes on bucket boundaries; it requires the same host/PID/command to lead with `D` in three consecutive samples. Treat this as a 15-minute sampled-persistence policy, not a Linux threshold or evidence of continuous blockage.
visualization: Use an active-candidates table with host, PID, command, user, observed states, first/last bucket, and sampled span. Add a drilldown showing each selected process-state sample and a host panel correlating disk latency, filesystem or network-storage errors, blocked-task messages, and service health. Keep a separate collection-freshness and parsed-row-count panel; never render missing snapshots as healthy state or describe the ten-minute first-to-last sample span as continuous blocked duration.
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on classifies `sourcetype=ps` as Performance data, but CIM Performance 6.4 has no per-process state or persistent blocked-task dataset. No equivalent accelerated `tstats` search is claimed. Endpoint process-start data is also not equivalent to repeated Linux scheduler-state snapshots, so the raw table and add-on-specific `STAT`/`S` fields are required.

knownFalsePositives:
A leading `D` is a real sampled process state, not a fabricated match. The alert can still be expected, misleading, or unactionable in these situations:

1. **Approved backup, snapshot, or storage maintenance** — Backup agents, database checkpoints, filesystem freeze/thaw work, and array or volume maintenance can legitimately leave a task waiting across several polls. Correlate the exact process, mount, maintenance ticket, storage latency, and bounded change window before suppressing it.

2. **Known network-filesystem or device outage already under response** — NFS, iSCSI, FUSE, multipath, removable-media, and device-driver problems can create persistent D-state tasks while a parent incident is active. Deduplicate against that incident, but continue recording affected processes and hosts; do not globally hide the signal.

3. **Intentional blocked-task or resilience test** — A controlled fault-injection exercise can deliberately reproduce uninterruptible waits. Require the named test owner, exact hosts and commands, start/end epochs, and change identifier. Expire the exception automatically.

4. **PID reuse or command ambiguity** — The supplied process snapshot has no reliable start-time field, and command text can be truncated. A process that exits and a replacement that receives the same PID and command could bridge the three samples. Confirm `/proc/<pid>/stat` start time and service restart history before claiming one continuous task identity.

5. **Replayed, duplicated, or malformed snapshots** — Duplicate input stanzas, replayed events, a removed table header, or a locally modified `ps.sh` can distort extraction. The search selects the latest raw event in each bucket and collapses duplicate identity rows, but collection-health and raw-event review remain required.

6. **Container namespace mismatch** — The host PID and command can differ from the workload operator's namespace. Resolve the host PID through cgroup and namespace information before routing the incident to a pod or container owner.

**Safe suppression:** preserve the base result, then apply an owner-approved lookup keyed by exact `host` and stable `process_name`, with `start_epoch`, `end_epoch`, `reason`, `ticket`, and `approver`. Reject host-wide wildcards, PID-only rules, and non-expiring entries. A suppression changes notification policy; it does not make the sampled D state false.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and interpretation boundary

Install a currently supported release of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) on every Linux Universal Forwarder that will collect process snapshots. Deploy the add-on's parsing and search-time knowledge to the tiers required by the local Splunk topology, and check the current Splunkbase compatibility table before installation or upgrade. The listing warns that version 6.0 changed default indexes and configuration files, so test upgrades outside production. The operations search role needs read access to the selected operating-system index and permission to schedule this search; it does not need broad administrative access.

Linux `ps` describes `D` as uninterruptible sleep, usually I/O, and `/proc/<pid>/stat` exposes the same one-character state. That label is not a root-cause code. A task may be waiting below the application in a local filesystem, block layer, network filesystem, device driver, page fault, kernel lock path, or another subsystem. The task normally cannot handle ordinary signals until the kernel wait completes, but this alert must not claim that a sampled process is permanently unkillable. Three snapshots also do not prove continuous D state between polls. The catalogue policy is: observe the same host, PID, and command leading with `D` in three selected five-minute snapshots. This is a tunable sampled-persistence rule, not a threshold published by Linux, procps, or Splunk.

## Step 1 — Configure data collection

Use the `ps.sh` scripted event input shipped with the add-on; do not replace it with an invented modular input or label the Universal Forwarder itself as Splunkbase 617. Copy only the exact installed stanza from `Splunk_TA_nix/default/inputs.conf` into `Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`, because Splunk recommends against copying the whole default file. Preserve the installed script path and source type, then set the collection policy explicitly. A five-minute example is:

```ini
[script://./bin/ps.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 300
index = os
```

`interval=300` and `index=os` are this implementation's choices, not claimed add-on defaults. Change the input and SPL together if governance selects another index. Each execution emits a complete process table, so estimate volume on high-process-count hosts before fleet rollout; shortening the interval can increase indexed volume and script overhead materially. Follow Splunk's documented script execution and operating-system privilege guidance rather than granting the forwarder unrestricted sudo.

After deployment, inspect the effective configuration with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`. Search `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m` and inspect `_raw`: each event must retain one table header and its aligned process rows. Then run `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m | multikv | table _time host PID STAT S COMMAND USER`. Current Linux add-on output uses `PID`, `STAT`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`. The add-on's field mapping documents legacy `S` as the predecessor of raw `STAT`, so the SPL coalesces `STAT`, `S`, and lower-case local aliases but treats `STAT` as canonical. `STAT` can contain modifier characters after the primary state; a value such as `D<` is therefore detected with `^D`, not equality to the single character `D`.

On a staging host, compare the same collection instant with `ps -eo user:32,pid,stat,wchan:32,lstart,comm,args --sort=pid`. Allow for execution, forwarding, and indexing delay. Spot-check healthy `R` and `S` rows as well as any `D` row, and verify PID, state, user, and command after `multikv`. Record command truncation or local edits to `ps.sh`, because both change process identity and supportability. If no natural D-state task is present, do not create one on production merely to test the alert; use isolated synthetic table events.

## Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_process_d_state_persistence_15m`. Schedule it every five minutes exactly on five-minute boundaries and trigger when the result count is greater than zero. The explicit `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m` range selects three closed five-minute buckets and leaves one bucket for normal arrival delay. Measure actual end-to-end latency before reducing that delay. If the scheduler is not aligned to five-minute boundaries, fix the schedule or redesign the bounds and rerun all controls.

The first `eval` preserves each raw event's exact timestamp as `snapshot_time`. `bin` assigns the raw event to a five-minute bucket. `eventstats max(snapshot_time)` is deliberately executed before `multikv`, so only the latest raw process-table event for each host and bucket is selected. This prevents multiple polls in one bucket from inflating persistence and ensures that an earlier parseable event is not silently substituted for a later malformed table. `multikv` then expands only the selected table into process rows.

The normalization step accepts current and documented legacy field names, converts PID to a string, uppercases the state, and provides explicit placeholders only for optional display fields. The `where` rejects headers and malformed PIDs. The first `stats` collapses duplicate rows for one host/PID/command in one selected snapshot. The second aggregation counts observed buckets and buckets whose state starts with `D`. The final gate requires three observations, three D observations, and a 600-second first-to-last bucket span. That span proves consecutive five-minute sample positions; it is ten minutes between first and last sample, covering a 15-minute three-snapshot policy. It is not a measured continuous blocked duration.

The process identity is `host + PID + COMMAND`. It prevents unrelated D-state tasks on one host from being combined, unlike a host-level event count, but it cannot fully prevent restart/PID-reuse collisions because the supplied current fields do not include process start time. Do not remove command from the grouping, aggregate only by host, or count raw `ps` events as blocked processes. If a reliable boot ID and process-start tick are mandatory, build and validate a separate approved collector rather than pretending those fields exist here.

The add-on classifies `ps` as Performance data, but CIM Performance 6.4 has no per-process scheduler-state dataset. An Endpoint process-start record is not a repeated state snapshot. For that reason this sidecar intentionally has no `cimSpl`; enabling Endpoint acceleration and searching a fabricated `process_state` field would create an unsupported detection.

## Step 3 — Validate parsing, snapshot selection, and thresholds

Build controls as complete aligned tables with the same header and spacing as an actual add-on event. Testing only pre-populated scalar fields skips the `multikv` behavior and is insufficient. For the positive control, place the three snapshots described in `controlTest` into adjacent closed buckets. Use the same PID, command, and user, with states `D`, `D<`, and `Ds`, and include healthy rows. Run a copy of the SPL against the isolated index with fixed absolute bounds. Expect one row, three observed buckets, three D-state buckets, observed states beginning with D, and a ten-minute sample span.

For the negative control, change the middle state to `S`. Before the final `where`, verify three observations but only two D-state buckets; after it, expect zero rows. Next rotate the D-state condition among three different PIDs and confirm no identity reaches three D buckets. Put the text `D` or `disk-wait` in a healthy process command and confirm command text is never interpreted as state. Add a missing-snapshot test and expect `observed_buckets=2`. Finally, put two raw snapshots in one bucket with different timestamps and confirm only rows from the later event survive the pre-`multikv` selection.

There is no Linux vendor inventory UI for this procfs state. Do not compare with a vendor dashboard as if it were authoritative; compare at least three staging snapshots with the on-host `ps` command. Confirm selected event timestamps, parsed row counts, and leading-state modifiers. Track source health separately with a last-seen search and a parsed-row-count trend; a no-result persistence search cannot distinguish a healthy host from a silent collector. This review is documentation-only. It did not execute the collector, index a fixture, run the SPL in Splunk, or validate a production platform/add-on combination. Keep `status=draft` until those checks and an SME review occur.

## Step 4 — Operationalize, investigate, visualize, and preserve evidence

Route a result to Linux platform operations and the owning service team. Deduplicate by host, PID, and command for no more than one search interval while retaining each scheduled result for trend and evidence. Do not automate `kill -9`, a service restart, filesystem unmount, storage failover, or host reboot from this alert. A task in D state may not process the signal until its wait returns, and disruptive action without dependency context can worsen an outage or destroy diagnostics.

On the host, first confirm that the PID still exists with `ps -p <pid> -o pid,ppid,user,stat,wchan:32,lstart,comm,args`. Compare `lstart` and `/proc/<pid>/stat` start information with deployment and service-restart records to detect PID reuse. Inspect `/proc/<pid>/wchan` where permissions allow, then correlate the wait channel and timestamp with kernel logs, filesystem errors, NFS or iSCSI client messages, multipath state, block-device latency, storage-array events, cgroup pressure, and application health. `wchan` is a clue, not a complete stack trace. Escalate to the responsible storage, network, device, or application owner based on evidence rather than assuming every D state is a disk failure.

If the incident runbook permits blocked-task diagnostics, an experienced operator may use the kernel's documented Magic SysRq `w` command through the approved console or `/proc/sysrq-trigger`. Treat that as a privileged production action: verify local policy and kernel settings, capture output safely, and never have Splunk invoke it automatically. Prefer established support procedures and vendor diagnostics on critical systems.

Display the current candidate table, a drilldown of selected state samples, and same-host I/O and service-health context. Add an independent panel showing last raw `ps` event, snapshots per bucket, and parsed process-row counts. Restrict raw command arguments because applications sometimes expose credentials or tenant data in command lines. Preserve the saved search, schedule, alert result, three source snapshots, collection-health result, and incident notes under the operations retention policy. Record whether the PID/start-time check, wait-channel review, and root-cause correlation were completed.

## Step 5 — Troubleshooting and safe suppression

No `ps` events usually means the supplied input remains disabled, the add-on is absent on the collection forwarder, execution requirements are unmet, data is routed to another index, or the search role lacks access. Use `btool`, the forwarder's `splunkd.log`, and the add-on's documented troubleshooting workflow to isolate configuration, execution, forwarding, and authorization. Raw tables without process fields usually mean the header or alignment was altered, search-time knowledge is missing, the source type changed, or an ingest transform split the table. Repair extraction rather than searching arbitrary raw text for ` D `.

If only `S` appears, the legacy mapping is in use and the SPL supports it. If state values are words such as `sleeping` rather than procps letters, a local collector changed the contract; document and validate a separate normalization instead of assuming equivalence. If an indexed PID is absent on the host, compare timestamps and collection latency before concluding that data is stale. If counts differ from on-host `ps`, inspect PID namespaces, duplicate input stanzas, event truncation, command truncation, and whether the process changed state between the two observations.

The primary SPL deliberately contains no exception lookup. For approved backup or fault-injection windows, preserve the base match and then apply a separately governed lookup keyed by exact host and stable command, active only between approved start and end epochs. Require owner, reason, ticket, and approver, and review suppressed matches. Never use a permanent whole-host exclusion, a PID-only exception, or a command substring shared by unrelated services. Expire each entry automatically and revalidate after kernel, storage, filesystem, add-on, or application changes.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for a program that repeatedly appears stuck waiting deep inside the operating system. Seeing the same program this way several times helps the team investigate a serious storage, device, or system problem without sounding an alarm for every brief wait.
